Bicycle Accidents in Washington: Where You Are Allowed to Ride, the Passing Rule, and Who Pays

Justin D. Leigh, Attorney-at-Law·8 min read·October 27, 2026

A driver came past you close enough to move the air, then turned right across your front wheel, and told the responding officer that you came out of nowhere and that bikes belong on the sidewalk. You are at the emergency department with a broken collarbone and a frame that is now scrap. Almost everything a driver believes about where a bicycle is allowed to be is written down in Washington, and most of it is the opposite of what they told the officer.

A bicycle on the roadway has the rights and the duties of a vehicle

RCW 46.61.755(1) says every person riding a bicycle upon a roadway shall be granted all of the rights and shall be subject to all of the duties applicable to the driver of a vehicle, except for the special bicycle regulations in RCW 46.61.750 through 46.61.780 and except for provisions that by their nature cannot apply.

That is the whole frame of a bicycle case. You are not a guest in the lane. The driver owed you what they owed any other vehicle, and the right-of-way rules that would govern a car turning across your path govern that same turn across a bicycle.

RCW 46.61.755(2) handles the other half. A person riding on a sidewalk or crosswalk is granted all the rights and subject to all the duties of a pedestrian. So the cyclist on a sidewalk is not an outlaw, and RCW 46.61.261(1) requires drivers to yield to a bicycle on a sidewalk, while requiring the rider to yield to pedestrians there.

How far right do I actually have to ride?

This is the argument in most of these cases, and RCW 46.61.770(1) answers it. A cyclist moving slower than the normal flow of traffic rides as near to the right side of the right through lane as is safe, with four exceptions written into the statute.

You may leave the right edge while preparing to turn or turning. You may use a dedicated right turn lane when approaching an intersection where right turns are permitted, even if you do not intend to turn right. You may move left while overtaking another bicycle or vehicle. And under subsection (1)(d), you may move when reasonably necessary to avoid unsafe conditions, which the statute defines to include fixed or moving objects, parked or moving vehicles, bicyclists, pedestrians, animals, and surface hazards.

That fourth exception is broad and it is what a door zone, a storm grate, broken pavement, or a row of parked cars falls under. RCW 46.61.770(3) separately permits use of the shoulder or any designated bicycle lane, and RCW 46.61.770(4) tells a rider in a single narrow lane to move far enough right to facilitate an overtaking vehicle unless conditions make that unsafe. RCW 46.61.770(5) allows riding two abreast, and no more than two, except on paths set aside for bicycles.

The three-foot rule, and what the Legislature changed in 2025

RCW 46.61.110(2) governs a driver overtaking a person on a bicycle in the right lane, on the right shoulder, or in a bicycle lane, and it was amended most recently in 2025.

On a roadway with two or more lanes going the driver's direction, the driver must move completely into a lane to the left of the right lane before passing, and stay there until safely clear. That is not a suggestion to give room. It is a lane change.

On a road with only one lane in the direction of travel, the driver must reduce to a speed that is safe for passing relative to the cyclist's speed and pass at a safe distance, where practicable of at least three feet, to clearly avoid contact. If there is not enough room on the left to do that, the driver must move completely into the oncoming lane when it is safe and lawful to do so.

RCW 46.61.110(2)(b) adds a fine equal to the base penalty on top of it, unwaivable except on a finding of indigency, and (c) sends it to the vulnerable roadway user education account. A traffic fine is not civil liability and no infraction decides a claim, but the standard of care in that subsection is written in unusually concrete terms, and concrete is what a liability case runs on.

Tell me about your situation

What about the helmet, the lights, and the sidewalk?

Expect all three to be raised and none of them to be what the insurer suggests.

Washington's helmet statute, RCW 46.37.530, is written for motorcycles, mopeds, and motor-driven cycles. Where it mentions bicycles it does so by pointing outward, directing riders of electric-assisted bicycles and motorized foot scooters to comply with laws and regulations related to the use of bicycle helmets. Whether a helmet was required where you were riding is therefore a local ordinance question that differs by city and county, and it is worth checking against the actual ordinance rather than against what anybody assumes.

Equipment and sidewalk rules work the same way as every other traffic statute here. Under RCW 5.40.050, breaking a statute, ordinance, or administrative rule is not negligence per se but may be considered as evidence of negligence, and the four exceptions that remain negligence per se do not include anything about bicycles. So riding without a light after dark is evidence a jury weighs against the rest of the case.

And under RCW 4.22.005, contributory fault reduces an award proportionately and does not bar it. A rider found twenty percent at fault recovers eighty percent. RCW 4.22.015 directs the comparison to consider both the nature of the conduct and how much it actually caused, which is the answer to a defense built on a missing taillight in a daylight collision.

Who pays when a car hits a bicycle

The driver's liability policy is the obvious one and it is frequently not enough. Washington's minimum limits are often well short of what a surgically repaired clavicle, a head injury, or three months away from work actually costs.

So look at your own auto policy even though you were on a bicycle. RCW 48.22.030(2) requires underinsured motorist coverage on auto policies issued in this state, reaching underinsured vehicles, hit-and-run vehicles, and phantom vehicles. The statute writes in an exception for a person operating or occupying a motorcycle or motor-driven cycle. A bicycle is neither, so that carve-out does not reach a cyclist.

Personal injury protection is the medical side of the same page. RCW 48.22.085(1) requires it to be offered as an optional coverage on every automobile liability policy issued or renewed here, and RCW 48.22.085(2) lets a named insured reject it in writing. Whether it reaches you while you are on a bicycle depends on the policy language, which is a reason to read the policy rather than guess at it.

If the car never touched you, which is common when a driver forces a rider into a curb or a ditch, RCW 48.22.030(8) is the provision to know. A phantom vehicle claim requires that the facts be corroborated by competent evidence other than your own testimony, and that the accident be reported to the appropriate law enforcement agency within seventy-two hours. Both conditions are easy to fail while you are still in a hospital.

How long do I have to bring a bicycle accident claim in Washington?

Three years, under RCW 4.16.080(2), which sets a three-year limit for any other injury to the person or rights of another and runs from the date of the crash.

RCW 4.16.190 excludes from the limitation period the time a claimant was under eighteen. A great many bicycle injuries are to children, and their clock is not their parents' clock.

A claim against a city, county, transit agency, or the state has a separate step before suit and a much shorter deadline for it, which the article on claims against government entities covers. That is the ordinary posture for a crash caused by road surface or by a trail or bike lane design.

Where this goes wrong

The bicycle is thrown away. The frame, the wheel, and the damaged components record the direction and force of the impact, and they are evidence long after the bruises are gone.

Nobody preserves the data. A bike computer, a phone, or a watch often holds speed and position in the seconds before the crash, and that record is usually the only neutral witness.

The collision report repeats the driver's belief that bikes are not allowed in the lane, nobody checks it against RCW 46.61.755 and RCW 46.61.770, and that belief becomes the frame of the claim.

The no-contact case goes unreported for more than seventy-two hours, which is exactly what RCW 48.22.030(8)(b) requires.

A head injury is treated as resolved because the CT was clean. Post-concussive symptoms declare themselves over months and belong in the medical record as they do.

No one reads the rider's own auto policy, and the case settles against the driver's minimum limits while underinsured motorist coverage sits unused.

What a lawyer does here

Early work decides most of these. Getting the bicycle and the gear into storage before anybody discards them. Pulling device data while it exists. Finding the business or transit camera that sees the intersection, which is normally overwritten inside a month. Reading the collision report against RCW 46.61.755 and RCW 46.61.770 rather than accepting its conclusions, because an officer's narrative is evidence and not a ruling on the law. Locating every policy that reaches you, including those on cars you were not riding in. And giving you a straight answer about where your own conduct is a real problem in the case rather than a bluff, since that is what the claim is actually worth.
